title: A system that writes measurably more successful fundraising letters
subtitle: I analyzed every past mailing of a donor-funded nonprofit, found what separated the strong letters from the weak, and turned that research into an AI system. With a writer's input and guidance, it writes measurably more successful letters.

card.title: Fundraising letters that are measurably more successful
card.line: An AI system built on research into every past mailing, guided by a writer's input.

team: Solo, end to end: analysis, prompt design, prototype, Claude skill

sections.headline: A system that writes measurably more successful fundraising letters
sections.subtext: A donor-funded nonprofit raises money with letters across the year. I built it an AI system that writes measurably more successful ones. The writer brings the input and guidance; the system brings what I found by measuring every main mailing on record against its own month.

sections.headline: Research into every past letter, built into a system that writes the next one

metrics.label: The setting
metrics.value: A donor-funded nonprofit that raises money with letters across the year. The working assumption was that the calendar decided which letters would do well.

metrics.label: My part
metrics.value: Solo, end to end: the research into past mailings, a Claude Project that writes with the writer, a web prototype, and a Claude skill for follow-up content.

metrics.label: What changed
metrics.value: Letters written with the system are measurably more successful, and the first one was already a success. It rests on one finding: many of the strongest letters came from months the averages called weak. No amounts are published.

metrics.label: Three takeaways
metrics.value: Compare each result with its own baseline before you look for patterns. Check what you find against what the field already knows. Build the findings into the system that writes.

sections.headline: Two letters, the same month, opposite results
sections.content:
The analysis starts as a table: every main mailing on record, each result put on a common basis so a large mailing and a small one can be compared.

Two rows come from the same month. One letter did far better than that month's average. The other did far worse.

The calendar could not explain that.

images.alt: Explanatory illustration: one mailing above its period average and another below the same average. Bar lengths are schematic, not measured data.
images.caption: Illustration of the comparison, not the organization’s results. The bars are schematic: the same period can contain letters above and below its average. No amounts or letter excerpts are shown.

sections.headline: Fundraising by the calendar hides the letters that beat it
sections.content:
Planning letters by the month is the obvious move, and the averages back it up: some months raise more than others. Stop there, and all the calendar gives you is a send date.

The donations a weak letter fails to raise don't show up in any average. If you write these letters, what goes in them is the question you face every time, from the first line.

sections.headline: The prevailing theory was the calendar
sections.content:
By the averages, a few months looked like the reliable drivers of a strong result, and the planning followed the calendar.

It was a reasonable reading of the averages. It just couldn't explain why some letters in a weak month did far better than others in a strong one.

sections.headline: Measured against its own month, every letter told a different story
sections.content:
So I stopped comparing letters with each other and compared each one with the average for its own month, across every year on record. That changed the picture.

Many of the strongest letters came from months the averages called weak, and nearly every month had letters well above and well below its own average.

images.alt: Illustration with invented values. Left: an average result per period, where one period looks clearly strongest. Right: each individual letter against its own period's average; in every period some letters land well above and some well below that average.
images.caption: Illustration, values invented. It shows the shape of the finding, not the organization's data: by the calendar one period looks like the answer, but against its own period, letters in every period land well above and well below the average.

sections.headline: From seasonality to what made the difference, in five steps
sections.content: The order mattered. Each step only made sense once the one before it had removed a false signal.

steps.label: Normalize
steps.description: Every mailing as its return per thousand letters sent, so mailings of different sizes could sit side by side.

steps.label: Find the season
steps.description: Monthly averages gave the calendar's own effect: some months simply raise more than others.

steps.label: Take the season out
steps.description: Each letter against its own month's average. Only now could a letter from a weak month be compared fairly with one from a strong month.

steps.label: Sort into three bands
steps.description: Average performers, outperformers and underperformers. The interesting work happens at the two ends.

steps.label: Ask what made the difference
steps.description: What the outperformers did that the others didn't, compared with the voice-and-tone analysis, the writing handbook and general fundraising best practice.

sections.headline: A concrete need beat an abstract mission
sections.content:
Once the season was out of the way, what separated the strong letters lined up with what fundraising practice has long held: a concrete, tangible need beats an abstract mission.

The last step was that check against general fundraising best practice. A pattern in a handful of letters is a hunch until something outside them backs it up, so only patterns the wider field also supports went into the system.

sections.headline: The research became a system that writes the letter with you
sections.content:
I put the findings together with the writing guidelines into a Claude Project, an AI workspace with its own standing instructions. The system carries what the strong letters did. The writer brings the input and guidance no table can supply. So it asks questions first, drafts from the answers and checks things along the way. One of its seasonal rules says what the research found: the text decides, not the month.

I also built a web prototype for the same flow, and a Claude skill that carries a finished letter's message into follow-up content for other channels. All four pieces are mine: the analysis, the Claude Project, the prototype and the skill.

images.alt: Explanatory workflow: past mailing patterns, writing guidelines and fundraising practice feed a system that asks, drafts and checks, guided by the writer's input. The result is measurably more successful letters, and a Claude skill carries them into follow-up content.
images.caption: Explanatory illustration, not a product screenshot. It maps the research, the Claude Project, the web prototype and the follow-up skill. No donor information, private results or original letter copy is shown.

sections.headline: Letters written with it are measurably more successful
sections.content:
With a writer's input and guidance, the system writes letters that measurably do better. The first letter written with it was already a success.

The organization keeps its numbers private, so no amounts or results appear here, the chart above is an illustration with invented values, and the organization stays unnamed.

sections.headline: Those two rows are still in the table
sections.content:
They no longer look like noise.

What separates them is now built into the system that writes the next letter.

sections.headline: What to check before your next appeal

steps.label: Compare each result with its own baseline before you look for patterns.
steps.description: A calendar average hides the letters that beat their month. Measure each one against its season first, then sort into average, over and under.

steps.label: Check what you find against what the field already knows.
steps.description: Your own top performers are a small sample. Where they agree with general fundraising best practice, trust the pattern. Where they don't, test it before you build on it.

steps.label: Build the findings into the system that writes.
steps.description: Turn the findings and your writing guidelines into questions and checks, not a one-shot prompt. The writer brings the input and guidance; the system brings the evidence.

sections.headline: Without consistent results, there is nothing to analyze yet
sections.content: If you have only a handful of mailings, or results you can't put on a common basis, the analysis has nothing to stand on. Start by recording results the same way every time; the system can wait.

The system won't draft until it has asked its questions, and it learned what to ask from letters that beat their month. If you raise money with letters, measuring your own against their season is a good place for us to start. Get in touch.

Solo end to end.
